q: 1. The direction of shear stress is
explain: Shear stress can act in both horizontal and vertical planes depending on the loading conditions and the orientation of the cross-section being analyzed.

q: 2. The state of pure shear stress is produced by
options: tension in one direction and equal compression in perpendicular direction
equal tensions in two directions at right angles
equal compression in two directions at right angles
explain: Pure shear at 45° is equivalent to equal tension and compression at right angles on the original planes; hence tension in one direction with equal compression perpendicular to it produces a state of pure shear.

q: 3. The direction of normal stress is
explain: By definition, normal stress acts perpendicular (normal) to the surface of the cross-section or failure plane.

q: 4. The direction of shear stress is
explain: Unlike normal stress, shear stress acts tangential or parallel to the surface of the plane.

q: 5. The actual numerical value of tensile stress (engineering stress) is .............. than the theoretical stress
explain: Engineering stress is calculated using the original cross-sectional area, whereas theoretical (true) stress accounts for the reduction in area during tension.

q: 6. Allowable stress in steel is less than
explain: For safety, the allowable or working stress is always kept significantly lower than the yield stress of the material to prevent permanent deformation.

q: 7. According to Hook's law, which one is wrong?
explain: Hooke's Law states Stress = E × Strain. Therefore, MoE × Stress = Strain is mathematically incorrect.

q: 8. The property by which a body returns to its original shape after removal of the force, is called
explain: Elasticity is defined as the property of a material to regain its original shape and size once the deforming force is removed.

q: 9. Stress is directly proportional to strain within elastic limit is given by
explain: This fundamental principle of elasticity was established by Robert Hooke.

q: 10. The property of a material by which is can be drawn to smaller section, due to tension, is called
explain: Ductility is the property that allows a material to be drawn into thinner sections (like wires) under tensile stress without fracturing.

q: 11. Elasticity of a body is defined
options: the property by which a body returns to its original shape after removal of load
the property by which a body don't returns to its original shape after removal of load
the property by which a body undergoes deformation even after removal of load
explain: Elasticity is the physical property that allows a material to return to its original dimensions after the unloading process.

q: 12. The property of a material by which it can be beaten or rolled into thin plates, is called
explain: Malleability is the property that allows a material to be hammered or rolled into thin sheets, typically under compressive forces.

q: 13. Elasticity of a body is
options: the ratio of stress to strain
the resistance to the force acting
explain: Elasticity represents the internal resistance of the material molecules to being separated by an external force.

q: 14. As the elastic limit reaches, tensile strain
options: increases in proportion to the stress
decreases in proportion to the stress
explain: Near the elastic limit, the stress-strain curve starts to flatten, meaning strain increases much faster than the corresponding increase in stress.

q: 15. The stress necessary to initiate yielding, is considerably
options: more than that necessary to continue it
less than that necessary to continue it
more than that necessary to stop it
less than that necessary to stop it
explain: The upper yield point (stress to initiate yielding) is higher than the lower yield stress required to sustain/continue the yielding process.

q: 16. Stress in a member subjected to a force is
options: the ratio of modulus of elasticity to strain
the product of modulus of elasticity and strain
the resistance to the force acting
sum of strain and modulus of elasticity
explain: According to the constitutive relation σ = Eε, stress is the product of the modulus of elasticity and strain.

q: 17. The phenomenon of slow extension of materials having constant load, i.e. increasing with the time is called
explain: Creep is defined as the slow, time-dependent increase in strain of a material under a constant sustained load.

q: 18. Young's modulus is the ratio of the normal stress to the
options: reciprocal of normal strain within elastic limit
explain: Young's modulus is valid only within the proportional limit where the stress-strain curve is linear.

q: 19. Modulus of rigidity is the ratio of
explain: The modulus of rigidity (G) is the ratio of shear stress to the corresponding shear strain.

q: 20. In any member of structure system, the strain does not effect the size of member
explain: Shear strain involves a change in shape (angle) rather than a change in dimensions or volume.

q: 21. Plasticity of a body is
options: the ratio of stress to strain
explain: While elasticity allows recovery of shape, plasticity is the property that allows permanent deformation.

q: 22. The ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain is called
explain: Poisson's ratio is a dimensionless constant representing the ratio of transverse contraction to longitudinal extension.

q: 23. The value of possion's ratio always remains
explain: For most engineering materials, Poisson's ratio typically ranges from 0 to 0.5, thus remaining less than one.

q: 24. If the stress in each cross-section of a pillar is equal to its working stress, it is called
explain: A 'body of equal strength' is one designed so that the stress is uniform (equal to the working/allowable stress) at every cross-section along its length.

q: 25. The percentage elongation of a material from a direct tensile test indicates
explain: High percentage elongation is a primary indicator that a material is ductile and can undergo significant plastic deformation.

q: 26. The percentage reduction of a material from a direct compressive test indicates
explain: Similar to elongation in tension, reduction in cross-sectional area in compression is a measure of ductility.

q: 27. The safe value of stress below which the material will not fail when subjected to reversal of stress is known as
explain: Endurance limit is the maximum stress that a material can withstand for an infinite number of cycles without failure.

q: 28. The property by which the metals deforms continuously at a slow rate without further increase in stress is called
explain: Creep is the time-dependent permanent deformation that occurs under constant stress, usually at high temperatures.

q: 29. A beam is said to be of uniform strength, if
options: B.M. is same throughout the beam
shear stress is same throughout the beam
deflection is same throughout the beam
bending stress is same at every section along its longitudinal axis
explain: A beam of uniform strength has a varying cross-section such that the maximum bending stress remains constant (equal to the allowable stress) at every section along its length.

q: 30. Toughness is
options: ability to absorb energy during plastic deformation
explain: Toughness represents the total energy a material can absorb before it actually fractures.

q: 31. The impact tests are used to determine
explain: Tests like Charpy and Izod measure the energy absorbed during impact, which defines the toughness.

q: 32. Along the neutral axis of a simply supported beam
explain: By definition, the neutral axis is the layer in a beam where bending-induced longitudinal strain is zero — fibres there neither stretch nor compress.

q: 33. The ratio of maximum instantaneous stress due to sudden loading to the maximum stress due to gradual loading will be
explain: Stress produced by a suddenly applied load is twice the stress produced by the same load applied gradually.

q: 34. What is tenancy?
explain: Tenacity (often misspelled as tenancy) refers to the ultimate tensile strength of a material.

q: 35. Simple bending equation is
explain: This is the standard Euler-Bernoulli bending equation relating moment, inertia, stress, and curvature.

q: 36. In a composite bar the load distribution among different materials of which it is made is based on the assumption the all the materials will have
explain: In composite bars, the primary assumption for compatibility is that all components undergo the same amount of strain.

q: 37. The stress due to temperature change in a member depends on
explain: Thermal stress only develops if the expansion or contraction is restricted by the support conditions.

q: 38. Strain energy of a member may be defined as work done on it
explain: Strain energy is the internal work stored in a material due to any form of deformation (tension, compression, etc.).

q: 39. Partial derivative of strain energy gives
explain: According to Castigliano's first theorem, the partial derivative of strain energy with respect to a load gives the deflection at that load.

q: 40. The strain energy stored in a specimen when strained within the elastic limit is known as
explain: Resilience is the capacity of a material to absorb energy when it is deformed elastically.

q: 41. The maximum strain energy stored in a specimen when strained within the elastic limit is known as
explain: Proof resilience is the maximum energy that can be stored without causing permanent deformation.

q: 42. Find the elongation of a rod if a load of p is applied on a rod having length, l c/s area, A and modulus of elasticity, E
explain: The standard formula for axial deformation is derived from Hooke's Law (σ = Eε), where strain ε = Δl/l and stress σ = p/A.

q: 43. Find the modulus elasticity of bar material (E) if c/s area of bar is A, length L, applied load P and elongation is Δ
explain: Rearranging the elongation formula Δ = PL/AE to solve for E gives E = PL/AΔ.

q: 44. The plane of maximum obliquity is inclined to major principal plane at an angle
explain: The plane of maximum obliquity (where the ratio of shear to normal stress, i.e. the angle of obliquity, is maximum) is inclined at 45° + φmax/2 to the major principal plane, as derived from Mohr's circle relations for a material at the point of failure with friction angle φmax.

q: 45. The amount of stress developed due to increase in temperature in case of SSB if l=10m, ΔT=10°C, A=5cm²
explain: As per key 1 but In a Simply Supported Beam (SSB), the beam is free to expand or contract. Since there is no restriction to thermal expansion, no thermal stress is developed.

q: 46. A member having cross section 5 cm × 5 cm is subjected to a tensile stress of 100 kg/cm², then the applied load should be
explain: Load = Stress × Area. Area = 5cm × 5cm = 25cm². Load = 100 kg/cm² × 25cm² = 2500 kg.

q: 47. Torsion is produced in a beam due to
options: eccentricity of load from centroidal axis
explain: Torsion occurs when a load is applied at a distance (eccentricity) from the longitudinal centroidal axis, creating a twisting moment.

q: 48. For ductile materials, the most appropriate failure theory is
explain: The maximum shear stress (Tresca) theory gives results that agree reasonably well with experimental yielding behavior of ductile materials, making it the most appropriate for such materials.

q: 49. Due to torsion moment beam get
explain: While bending moments cause curvature (bending), torsional moments specifically cause the cross-sections to rotate or twist relative to each other.

q: 50. Elasticity of a body is
options: the property by which a body returns to its original shape after removal of the load
the ratio of stress to strain
the resistance to the force acting
large deformability as in case of rubber
explain: Elasticity is fundamentally defined as the ability of a material to return to its original shape/size once the deforming load is removed.
